KLO: Critically examine how functional expertise, personality, cognitive bias and emotional conditions influence the interpretation of strategy.
Demonstrate shared strategic understanding and commitment across the leadership system.
Recognise the organisational conditions that strengthen or weaken strategic alignment.
Lead people through the changes the strategy requires, with deliberate attention to readiness, resistance and adoption.

SECTIONS.name: Intelligence

SECTIONS.name: Extrapolating
SECTIONS.heading: Where Does the Leadership Team Stand?

Assess the readiness of the people most affected by the changes the strategy requires.

SECTIONS.name: Integration

SECTIONS.name: Application

Demonstrate commitment through a behavioural change that strengthens collective alignment.

1.1.label: Reflection
1.1.prompt: In your current role, which filter (Mind or Heart) tends to shape your first response to a new strategic priority? What are the implications?

1.2.label: Reflection
1.2.prompt: Which of the Five Principles describes the most critical gap in your leadership team right now? What is the evidence for this?

1.3.label: Reflection — The event and the transition
1.3.prompt: Write down one change your strategy requires of a named group. You will carry this change through the rest of the unit. On the day it was announced, how far through your own transition were you and your fellow leaders, and how far were the people affected?

1.3.1.label: Reflection — The 3S Check
1.3.1.prompt: Write the Shift, the Stake and the Step for the change you are carrying through this unit. Which of the three would your people find hardest to say back, and why?

1.3.2.label: Reflection
1.3.2.prompt: Which SCARF trigger is most frequently activated in your organisation during strategy implementation? What is the observable evidence? What counter-strategy would address the root cause?

1.3.3.label: Reflection — The STAT Check
1.3.3.prompt: Run STAT for the change you are carrying through this unit. Which element is missing for the people it affects most? What is your evidence, and what is yours to supply?

1.3.4.label: Reflection
1.3.4.prompt: If you audited your last leadership review against the ACE-IT behaviours — where would you find the biggest gap between the ideal and the observable? What one behavioural change would create the most impact?

2.1.label: Reflection
2.1.prompt: Think of a time when you personally chose to go beyond compliance and genuinely committed to a strategic direction. What caused that shift? What would it take to create that same shift in your team?

2.2.label: Reflection
2.2.prompt: How much of your current leadership time is spent enforcing compliance? What is the opportunity cost of this?

2.3.label: Reflection — Installed and adopted
2.3.prompt: Name one change in your organisation that is installed and still awaiting adoption. Which check did it fail: Mind, Heart, Hands or Habit? What has the adoption gap cost so far?

3.1.label: Reflection — OCEAVL
3.1.prompt: Which of your own levels carries the highest risk for how you read and lead the strategy? Where has that risk already shown up?

4.1.label: Reflection — One voice
4.1.prompt: Choose one group in your organisation. List every change the leadership team is asking of it this quarter. How many are there? Which of the four commitments is weakest in your team today?

4.2.label: Reflection
4.2.prompt: What is the most important alignment conversation you need to have with a closely adjacent role in the next 30 days? What would that conversation need to address?

CLOSING_Q: Which ACE-IT behaviour in your record will be hardest for this leadership team to show, and what in the team’s OCEAVL profile makes it so?

OCEAVL.name: Openness
OCEAVL.desc: Curiosity, creativity, adaptability to new approaches

levels.dna: Prefers safe and familiar ideas. Waits for certainty before acting. May miss external shifts.
levels.risk: Decisions stall waiting for certainty; teams default to legacy approaches; market shifts recognised too late.
levels.resp: Introduce a 70% certainty rule. Force strategic reframing via clean-slate questions. Commission one “What If” scenario memo each cycle.
levels.rout: Clarity Trial; Zero-Base Huddle; Trend Rotation
rd: Clarity Trial
The team agrees to act when it is about 70% sure, and reviews the result afterwards.
Zero-Base Huddle
A short meeting that asks: if we were starting from nothing today, what would we do?
Trend Rotation
Members take turns to bring one outside trend and a short “What if” note on what it could mean.

levels.dna: Mixes routine and creativity well. Tests ideas when supported by evidence. Open to learning.
levels.risk: Avoidance of discomfort over time; evidence-heavy culture slows experimentation; improvements stay incremental.
levels.resp: Mandate one deliberately uncomfortable experiment per cycle. Require one judgement-based pilot. Ask what a 10× outcome would require.
levels.rout: The Stretch Sync; The Intuition Log; The Moonshot Minute
rd: The Stretch Sync
Each cycle the team picks one experiment that is uncomfortable on purpose, and reports back on it.
The Intuition Log
The team runs one pilot on judgement, records the reasoning, and checks it later against what happened.
The Moonshot Minute
A short slot in a meeting that asks what a result ten times bigger would require.

levels.dna: Enjoys new approaches. Quick to adapt. Multiple ideas compete simultaneously.
levels.risk: Too many ideas fragment focus; initiatives start without completing; priorities blur.
levels.resp: Enforce One In, One Out rule. Temporarily freeze new starts. Re-anchor every pivot to agreed strategic intent.
levels.rout: 48-Hour Validation; Finish Line Friday; The Anchor Check
rd: 48-Hour Validation
A new idea waits two days and must name the work it replaces before it is accepted.
Finish Line Friday
Each Friday the team reviews what was finished. New work waits until open work is closed.
The Anchor Check
Before any change of direction, the team states how it serves the agreed strategic intent.

levels.dna: Struggles to stay organised. May start tasks but not finish. Delivery is unpredictable.
levels.risk: Commitments missed; output quality varies; outcomes lack ownership.
levels.resp: Introduce a RAG status board. Mandate peer-review before closure. Assign a single named owner per key result.
levels.rout: Monday Commit; Quality Spot-Check; Ownership Stand-Up
rd: Monday Commit
Each Monday every member states their commitments for the week, and the team tracks them as red, amber or green.
Quality Spot-Check
A colleague reviews each piece of work before it is closed.
Ownership Stand-Up
A short meeting in which each key result is answered for by its one named owner.

levels.dna: Usually dependable but feels stress under sustained pressure. Tries to stay disciplined across many tasks.
levels.risk: Sustained workload erodes reliability; critical steps bypassed under pressure; long-term health traded for short-term delivery.
levels.resp: Actively rebalance demand to real capacity. Mandate checklists for high-risk tasks. Protect dedicated clean-up time.
levels.rout: Load Audit; Step-Check; Health Check
rd: Load Audit
The team compares the work asked of it with its real capacity, and moves or drops work to fit.
Step-Check
A checklist is used for every high-risk task, so that no step is skipped under pressure.
Health Check
Set time is protected to clear backlogs and repair what was rushed.

levels.dna: Very organised and structured. Wants things done perfectly and on time.
levels.risk: Over-planning delays action; perfectionism blocks “good enough”; teams freeze when plans change.
levels.resp: Explicitly authorise Plan B approaches. Impose strict time limits on planning. Define Minimum Viable Result.
levels.rout: Pivot Sprint; Speed-to-Action; MVR Audit
rd: Pivot Sprint
When a plan changes, the team is authorised to run a short Plan B and act on it.
Speed-to-Action
Planning has a fixed time limit. When it ends, the team acts.
MVR Audit
Before work starts, the team defines the Minimum Viable Result: the least that counts as good enough.

levels.dna: Quiet and reflective. Prefers small groups or time to think before speaking.
levels.risk: Critical insights remain unspoken; stress causes withdrawal; information is pulled not pushed.
levels.resp: Begin meetings with silent written input. Schedule intentional 1-on-1 reconnection. Enforce push-based reporting.
levels.rout: Digital Ink-Well; Pulse Check; Flash Update
rd: Digital Ink-Well
Meetings open with everyone writing their input in silence before anyone speaks.
Pulse Check
Leaders hold regular one-to-one conversations to reconnect with each member.
Flash Update
Each member sends a short update without being asked for it.

levels.dna: Comfortable mixing with people. Can balance talking and listening well.
levels.risk: Meetings drift into social discussion; consensus delays decisions; purpose slips.
levels.resp: Restrict updates to blockers, decisions, actions only. Appoint a final decision-maker per forum. Restate strategic intent at every start.
levels.rout: Outcome-Only Syncs; 51/49 Rule; Intent Intro
rd: Outcome-Only Syncs
Updates cover three things only: blockers, decisions and actions.
51/49 Rule
Each forum has one named person who makes the final call when views are split.
Intent Intro
Every meeting opens by restating the strategic intent it serves.

levels.dna: Loves people and energy in discussion. Enjoys leading from the front.
levels.risk: Dominant voices crowd out data; action runs ahead of evidence; competing agendas fragment effort.
levels.resp: Require senior leaders to speak last. Mandate data summary with all proposals. Resolve single most critical agenda overlap.
levels.rout: Rotating Facilitator; Evidence Gate; Synergy Sync
rd: Rotating Facilitator
A different member leads each meeting, and senior leaders speak last.
Evidence Gate
A proposal is discussed only when it comes with a summary of the data behind it.
Synergy Sync
The team names the one overlap between agendas that does the most damage, and resolves it.

levels.dna: Can be very direct or firm in views. May struggle with patience for others’ ideas.
levels.risk: Conflict turns defensive and erodes trust; ego overrides outcomes; toxic seams between departments.
levels.resp: Shift to Problem/Data/Options language. Ask whether behaviours are helping or harming outcomes. Force cross-functional task swaps.
levels.rout: Issue-Evidence-Options; Result-First Review; Seam Huddle
rd: Issue-Evidence-Options
A disagreement is stated in three parts: the issue, the evidence and the options.
Result-First Review
The team asks of its own behaviour: is this helping the result or harming it?
Seam Huddle
Members of two departments swap a task, then meet to fix the hand-over between them.

levels.dna: Works well with most people. Manages conflict calmly. Balances kindness and firmness.
levels.risk: Feedback delayed; issues avoided to preserve harmony; apparent agreement masks unresolved risks.
levels.resp: Challenge work while explicitly demonstrating care. Name the uncomfortable issue at the start of the meeting. Ask the team to identify reasons the plan might fail.
levels.rout: Stop-Start-Continue; Hard-Talk Slot; Pre-Mortem
rd: Stop-Start-Continue
Feedback is given in three parts: what to stop, what to start and what to continue.
Hard-Talk Slot
The uncomfortable issue is the first item in the meeting.
Pre-Mortem
Before a plan is approved, the team lists the reasons it might fail.

levels.dna: Kind and warm. Ready to help others. Sometimes avoids saying no to preserve peace.
levels.risk: Agreement given without genuine commitment; team over-commits; resentment builds beneath surface harmony.
levels.resp: Assign a formal Devil’s Advocate role. Require explicit capacity check before accepting new work. Use anonymous mechanisms to surface tensions.
levels.rout: Rotating Challenger; No-Log; Radical Candor Loop
rd: Rotating Challenger
One member, a different one each time, is given the job of arguing against the proposal.
No-Log
The team checks its capacity before it accepts new work, and keeps a record of what it declined.
Radical Candor Loop
Members raise tensions through an anonymous channel, and the team answers them in the open.

levels.dna: Feels emotions strongly. May react fast under stress. Can take criticism personally.
levels.risk: Stress triggers impulsive decisions; errors hidden due to fear; anxiety grows from information gaps.
levels.resp: Mandatory 24-hour pause before high-stakes decisions. Leaders model safety by sharing their own failures. Regular factual briefings during volatile periods.
levels.rout: Morning-After Review; Error-Share; Daily Truth
rd: Morning-After Review
A high-stakes decision waits a day and is reviewed the next morning before it is confirmed.
Error-Share
Leaders share a mistake of their own first, so that others feel safe to report theirs.
Daily Truth
In volatile periods, a short daily briefing gives the facts as they stand.

levels.dna: Usually calm but can feel stress in long pressure periods. Manages emotions most of the time.
levels.risk: Important emotional signals missed; calm leadership misread as indifference; stability delays necessary urgency.
levels.resp: Increase visible leadership presence. Use explicit empathy language. Deliberately introduce strategic urgency where required.
levels.rout: Pulse Audit; Human Sync; Burn Rate Review
rd: Pulse Audit
Leaders spend visible time with their teams and ask how people are coping.
Human Sync
A regular check-in in which leaders name what people are feeling and acknowledge it.
Burn Rate Review
The team reviews how fast time and resources are being used, and raises the pace where it is needed.

levels.dna: Stays calm and steady even in chaos. Rarely loses control or reacts emotionally.
levels.risk: Calm misread as emotional distance; problems overlooked because everything appears fine; frontline disconnect.
levels.resp: Explicitly acknowledge effort, strain, and contribution. Demand objective data proving safety and control. Spend regular time embedded in operations.
levels.rout: Gratitude Minute; Red-Team Audit; Frontline Friday
rd: Gratitude Minute
Meetings open with a named thank-you for effort, strain or contribution.
Red-Team Audit
A separate group tests the claim that all is under control, and asks for the data.
Frontline Friday
Leaders spend regular time working alongside frontline staff.

OCEAVL.name: Values Alignment
OCEAVL.desc: Consistency between stated values and lived behaviour

levels.dna: May act differently from the group’s shared values. Can seem unsure about what the team stands for.
levels.risk: Personal preference overrides shared values; different parts of the organisation operate under conflicting value systems; trust erodes.
levels.resp: Publicly pause work that violates stated values. Rotate cultural ambassadors across silos. Conduct a formal review of promises versus delivery.
levels.rout: Value Filter; Culture Stand-Up; Integrity Scorecard
rd: Value Filter
Work is tested against the stated values, and work that breaks them is paused in the open.
Culture Stand-Up
Culture ambassadors move between departments and report what they see in a short meeting.
Integrity Scorecard
A formal review compares what was promised with what was delivered.

levels.dna: Understands values but may bend them when under pressure.
levels.risk: Values deprioritised under pressure; values exist conceptually but not operationally; ethical standards applied inconsistently.
levels.resp: Actively spotlight examples of values in action. Link each value to at least one active performance metric. Reference values during difficult decisions.
levels.rout: Narrative Share; Value KPI Check; Decision Audit
rd: Narrative Share
Members tell short stories of the values being lived in real work.
Value KPI Check
Each value is tied to at least one live performance measure, and the measure is reviewed.
Decision Audit
After a hard decision, the team records which values it used to decide.

levels.dna: Strongly lives by the organisation’s values. Acts as role model.
levels.risk: Strong conviction slows adaptation; external perspectives excluded; judgement focuses on style over results.
levels.resp: Periodically reassess whether values still support strategy. Deliberately introduce outsider viewpoints. Anchor feedback in outcomes and values only.
levels.rout: Value Evolution; Diversity Huddle; Merit Sync
rd: Value Evolution
From time to time the team reviews whether its values still serve the strategy.
Diversity Huddle
An outsider is invited in to give a different view.
Merit Sync
Feedback is given on outcomes and values only.

OCEAVL.name: Learning Orientation
OCEAVL.desc: Growth mindset, openness to feedback, skill development

levels.dna: Feels nervous about feedback or change. Avoids new skills for fear of failing.
levels.risk: Capabilities decay as methods become outdated; feedback resisted because it threatens status; leaders do not invite feedback themselves.
levels.resp: Require one small new-tool experiment each month. Reframe mistakes as neutral learning data. Leaders explicitly ask for feedback first.
levels.rout: 10-Minute Teach; Post-Mortem Pulse; Reverse Feedback
rd: 10-Minute Teach
Each month a member tries one small new tool and shows the team what they learned, in a short slot.
Post-Mortem Pulse
After a mistake, the team records what happened and what was learned, with no blame.
Reverse Feedback
Leaders ask their team for feedback on themselves before they give any.

levels.dna: Likes learning when useful. Can lose interest in long or complex lessons.
levels.risk: Learning remains shallow and episodic; training does not translate into changed behaviour; teams fix symptoms and leave the causes.
levels.resp: Force reflection on root causes. Require a written application note after learning events. Apply Five Whys technique to failures.
levels.rout: Quarterly Growth Review; 7-Day Implementation; Root-Cause Sync
rd: Quarterly Growth Review
Each quarter the team looks back at what it learned and at the root causes of what went wrong.
7-Day Implementation
Within a week of a learning event, each member writes how they have applied it.
Root-Cause Sync
After a failure, the team asks “why?” five times to reach the cause.

levels.dna: Loves learning and shares knowledge freely. Enjoys experimenting with ideas and tools.
levels.risk: Excessive experimentation diffuses focus; teams outpace the organisation’s ability to absorb change; learning not institutionalised.
levels.resp: Cap learning and experimentation time deliberately. Slow learning cycles to match organisational readiness. Prevent new learning until existing lessons are embedded.
levels.rout: Playbook Build; Sync Cycle; Standard Build
rd: Playbook Build
Time for experiments is capped, and what was learned is written into a shared playbook.
Sync Cycle
New learning is released at the pace the organisation can absorb.
Standard Build
A lesson becomes the standard way of working before the next new idea is taken on.

OC_STEPS_F: They score themselves from 1 to 5 on each of the seven dimensions: 1 is strongly low, 3 is balanced and 5 is strongly high.
A score of 4 or 5 is High, 3 is Balanced, and 1 or 2 is Low. This gives the participant’s own level on each dimension.
They read their own profile. Each level carries a risk, a response and three routines that hold the response in place.
They select Submit to My Team’s Capstone. Print gives a copy of their own profile.
The level held by most members of a team is the team’s level for that dimension. The team’s profile appears in the team’s Capstone Blueprint once every member has submitted.
OC_STEPS_P: Score yourself from 1 to 5 on each of the seven dimensions: 1 is strongly low, 3 is balanced and 5 is strongly high. Work alone. Your scores are your own.
A score of 4 or 5 is High, 3 is Balanced, and 1 or 2 is Low. This gives your own level on each dimension.
Read your own profile. Each level carries a risk, a response and three routines that hold the response in place.
Select Submit to My Team’s Capstone. Your scores join your team’s profile.
The level held by most members of your team is the team’s level for that dimension. Your team’s profile appears in your team’s Capstone Blueprint once every member has submitted.
OC_EVERY: Every level carries a risk. A High level is a disposition to manage, as Low and Balanced are.

HOT.need: People need to know exactly what is changing.
HOT.why: The CEO sets the direction for the whole organisation. A direction is broad, and it is easy to announce one without saying which practice changes, for which group, from which date. People then cannot picture the change, and each team fills the gap with its own version.
HOT.trig: The change is announced as a direction, such as “we are becoming more customer-focused”. Nobody says which practice stops, which practice starts, for which group and from which date.
HOT.cues: People keep working the old way and call it by the new name. Three teams asked what is changing give three different answers.
HOT.cost: People cannot follow a change they cannot picture. Each team acts on its own version, and effort goes in different directions.

HOT.need: People need to see the reasoning, the progress and the constraints.
HOT.why: The CFO decides where the money goes, and every budget decision is a trade-off. A trade-off is uncomfortable to show, so the decision often reaches people without its reasons. People then read the cut as the real message about the change.
HOT.trig: A budget is cut, frozen or moved, and people are told the decision without the reason. Good results are shared quickly and setbacks are shared late.
HOT.cues: People say “Finance said no” and cannot explain why. Teams stop keeping their own figures up to date, because they never see what the figures are used for.
HOT.cost: People treat the change as a cost exercise that will pass. They keep the new practice while it is checked and drop it afterwards.

HOT.need: People need the hours to do the new work.
HOT.why: The COO turns the strategy into daily work. Each new practice looks small when it is added, and it is easy to add it to a day that is already full without taking any old work away. People then want the change and have no hours to do it.
HOT.trig: A new practice is added to the working day and nothing is taken away. The old targets and deadlines stay as they were.
HOT.cues: The new practice is done at the end of the day, or dropped on a busy day. People say “we will get to it when things calm down.”
HOT.cost: People who agree with the change still cannot do it. Their goodwill wears out, because they are asked for more than the day can hold.

HOT.need: People need to know how to do the new work.
HOT.why: The CHRO leads the building of capability. A briefing or a training session is easy to count as capability built. People have heard about the new work and have not yet practised it, so they make errors and go back to the old method.
HOT.trig: People attend a briefing or a training session and are then expected to perform. Nobody watches them do the new work and corrects them.
HOT.cues: Errors and rework rise. Everyone goes to the same one or two experts. People say “let me do it the old way to get it done.”
HOT.cost: People lose confidence in themselves and in the change, and the old way starts to look safer.

HOT.need: People need the systems and resources the new work depends on.
HOT.why: The CTO or CIO supplies the systems people work in every day. A new practice can be agreed long before the system, the form or the budget has changed to fit it. People then try the new way, find that the system still fits the old way, and build workarounds.
HOT.trig: The new practice starts before the system, the form or the access rights have been changed to support it.
HOT.cues: People keep their own spreadsheets beside the system. Work waits on another team for access or data.
HOT.cost: People do the work twice, once in the new way and once in the old. The extra effort turns willing people against the change.

HOT.need: People need a say in how the change is going.
HOT.why: The CMO shapes the message about the change. A strong message travels one way, from leaders to people, and it is easy to treat the message as the conversation. People then have nowhere to say how the change is going, and they stop owning it.
HOT.trig: The change is launched as a campaign: a town hall, emails and posters. People are told about it and are never asked how it is going.
HOT.cues: Meetings about the change are presentations, and people ask nothing. Asked why the change matters, they cannot say it in their own words.
HOT.cost: People stay spectators of the change, so it fades when the campaign ends.

HOT.need: People need to see the change applied evenly.
HOT.why: The CCO sets the targets and the rewards. People read every target and every reward as a signal of what is fair. When the change asks more of one team than of another, or the rewards still favour the old behaviour, people stop wanting it to succeed.
HOT.trig: The change asks more of one team than of another, or the targets and rewards still pay for the old behaviour.
HOT.cues: People ask “why us and never them?” They talk about the change in the corridor and say nothing in the meeting.
HOT.cost: People stop wanting the change to succeed. They do what is measured and hold back the rest.

HOT.need: People need permission to decide and act.
HOT.why: The CPO sets the approval rules for spend. A change often moves a decision closer to the front line, and the approval rule stays where it was. People then ask permission for what the change has asked them to do, and the decision travels back up.
HOT.trig: The change asks front-line people to decide for themselves, and the approval limits stay where they were. The first person who decides alone is overruled.
HOT.cues: Requests for approval rise. People ask “am I allowed to do this?” about the very thing the change asks of them.
HOT.cost: Decisions travel back up, and the new way runs slower than the old one. People conclude that the change is talk.

HOT.need: People need some control over how they do their own work.
HOT.why: The CRO sets the controls and the reporting. Each control is added for a sound reason, and each one takes some discretion from the people doing the work. As the controls add up, people feel they have lost control of their own work, and they comply without energy.
HOT.trig: New controls, sign-offs or reports arrive with the change, and people are given no choice in how they meet them.
HOT.cues: People do exactly what the rule says and nothing more. Forms are completed and questions stop.
HOT.cost: People comply and stop caring. The paperwork arrives, and the judgement and energy the change depends on are lost.

HOT.need: People need to know why the change matters to them.
HOT.why: The CSO holds the reasoning behind the strategy. That reasoning is usually stated as a benefit to the enterprise: growth, margin or position. A benefit that never reaches a team’s own work sounds like someone else’s reason, so people can describe the change and cannot say what it is for.
HOT.trig: The reason for the change is given as a benefit to the organisation, such as growth or margin. Nobody says what the team gains, or what it loses by staying as it is.
HOT.cues: People say “because head office said so.” They can describe the change and cannot say what it is for.
HOT.cost: People carry out the change while they are watched and set it aside under pressure. They have the instruction and are missing the reason.

TERMS.teach: Every role on a leadership team affects alignment in two ways at once. This part shows both for each role, side by side.
TERMS.czc: What a role brings so that the leadership team reads the strategy as one. The Converging Zone is the point where the separate views of each function come together into one shared reading. A role’s contribution is the part of that reading only that role can supply.
TERMS.ahz: The one place where a role is most likely to lose people as it does its normal work. It is one of the 17 elements of 3S, SCARF, STAT and ACE-IT taught in parts 1.3.1 to 1.3.4. It tells the leader which check the role puts at risk: people’s understanding (Mind), their willingness (Heart), their ability to act (Hands) or their follow-through (Habit).
TERMS.why: They come from the same work. The work that makes a role valuable to the team is the work that creates its hot zone. The CEO sets direction: that is the contribution. A direction announced in broad terms leaves people unsure what changes for them: that is the hot zone. A leader who knows both keeps giving the contribution and guards the hot zone.
lines: Why the role is inclined to it: how the role’s normal work creates the risk.
What sets it off: the action that starts the problem.
What is seen and heard: the signs that it has started.
What it costs: what people then do, and what the change loses.
TERMS.close: Read together, the hot zones of a team show where its changes are most likely to lose people’s minds and hearts.
TERMS.one: The Converging Zone is the point where the separate views of each function come together into one shared reading of the strategy. A leadership team that reaches it has Collective Intelligence, and the organisation hears one voice. The two columns show what people receive with it and without it.
TERMS.czc_p: What your role brings so that your leadership team reads the strategy as one. The Converging Zone is the point where the separate views of each function come together into one shared reading. Your contribution is the part of that reading only your role can supply.
TERMS.ahz_p: The one place where your role is most likely to lose people as it does its normal work. It is one of the 17 elements of 3S, SCARF, STAT and ACE-IT that you met in parts 1.3.1 to 1.3.4. It tells you which check your role puts at risk: people’s understanding (Mind), their willingness (Heart), their ability to act (Hands) or their follow-through (Habit).

G3.is: The Shift names the practice that ends and the practice that begins, for a named group, from a named date. It is concrete enough to be observed: someone watching the work could tell whether it is happening. A direction such as “more customer-focused” leaves every person to decide what it means, and each will decide differently.
G3.clear: “From March, agents resolve complaints on the first call.”
G3.mv: State the Shift as from and to: what stops, what starts, for whom, from when.

G3.q: “What do we gain if we change, and what do we lose if we stay as we are?”
G3.is: The Stake is why the change matters, and it has two sides. The gain says what the change is for. The loss says what standing still will cost. Both are needed, because people weigh a loss more heavily than an equal gain. A change described only by its benefits leaves the people affected holding the one visible loss: the practice they are asked to give up. Naming what is lost by staying put places a second loss on the scales. The Stake is stated in terms the affected group cares about. An enterprise benefit that never reaches their work reads as someone else’s reason.
G3.clear: “We keep the customers who now leave after a two-day wait. If we stay as we are, we keep losing them.”
G3.mv: State the gain and the loss together, in the group’s own terms.

G3.is: The Step is the person’s own part. It is said in the first person and is small enough to do next week. The Shift belongs to the organisation and the Step belongs to the person, so each role affected needs its own. A change with a clear Shift and no Step is understood as something that will happen to other people.
G3.clear: “I decide on the call, within my limit.”
G3.mv: Give each affected role its own Step, and ask people to say it back.

GA.def: Taking full ownership for results. Acknowledging missteps and driving corrective action.
GA.does: One named person owns the practice and its result.
GA.obs: Commitments tracked • Reviews end with named owners • “We missed it, here’s the fix” language common

GA.def: Staying anchored to agreed strategic intent even when pressure rises. Following through despite discomfort.
GA.does: The practice is kept when pressure rises and the old way is quicker.
GA.obs: Strategic priorities stay consistent • Leaders decline non-strategic work • Promises kept visibly

GA.def: Actively involving self and others in sense-making, dialogue, and execution. Listening to understand.
GA.does: People talk about how it is going and improve it together.
GA.obs: Team meetings are two-way • Feedback loops visible • People quote the shared “why”

GA.def: Acting consistently with values, facts, and truth — even when inconvenient. Declaring conflicts of interest early.
GA.does: Slips are reported as they are, and early.
GA.obs: Evidence cited before decisions • Values referenced in hard choices • Teams trust word matches deed

GA.def: Making reasoning, progress, and constraints visible to all stakeholders. Sharing challenges openly.
GA.does: Its results are visible to everyone the change affects.
GA.obs: Dashboards updated regularly • Decisions logged and accessible • “No surprises” culture evident

ASK.stake: What will the organisation gain if it changes, and what will it lose if it stays as it is?

ACE_ASK: The behaviour we expect from our leadership team
STEP1_ACT_F: The group reads the practices the strategy starts and stops. Each page shows the Start and Stop lists the group confirmed in Unit 3.
The group reads the guide in each card. It is the lesson from part 1.3.1.
The group agrees its Shift, Stake and Step for the strategy, and each participant writes them in the three boxes.
STEP2_ACT_F: The group reads its team OCEAVL profile, shown on each page once every member of the team has submitted their scores in part 3.1.
The group reads the guide in each card. It is the lesson from part 1.3.4.

For each behaviour, the group agrees what it expects to see the leadership team do so that the change in Step 1 holds. Where the team’s level carries a risk for this change, the group states the behaviour that answers it.
Each participant reads the record and selects Confirm. Print gives a copy of the record.
STEP1_GUIDE_F: Briefing: Each group works with the Start and Stop lists it confirmed in Unit 3 in view, and states one Shift, one Stake and one Step for its strategy.
Watch for: a Shift written as a direction. Ask what stops, what starts, for whom and from when.
Watch for: a Stake that gives the gain only. Ask what the organisation loses if it stays as it is.
Watch for: a Step written for the organisation. Ask each member to say their own part in the first person.
STEP2_GUIDE_F: Briefing: The group opens with its team OCEAVL profile. The profile shows the team’s level on each dimension, with its risk and its response.
Linking question: “Which level in your team’s profile carries the highest risk for this change? Which ACE-IT behaviour answers it?”
Watch for: a value written where a behaviour is asked for, such as “we will be accountable”. Ask what a colleague would see the leadership team do.
Watch for: behaviours expected of staff. The five boxes are for the leadership team’s own behaviour.
CHAIN: People first make sense of the strategy. They interpret what it means, what matters, what has changed, what is expected, and what risks or opportunities they see. This is where assumptions, mental models, expertise, past experience and bias shape the meaning people attach to the strategy.

People then experience the strategy emotionally. They may feel energised, uncertain, threatened, excluded, hopeful, tired or resistant. This emotional state affects trust, morale, psychological safety, engagement energy and the willingness to participate honestly in execution.

People then make choices and trade-offs. They decide what to prioritise, what to resource, what to protect, what to stop, what to challenge and what to support. This is where strategy becomes real through judgement, commitment, accountability and allocation of attention.

People finally act in ways that either carry the strategy forward or weaken it. Behaviour shows up in follow-through, handovers, routines, conversations, ownership, discipline and how people respond when execution becomes difficult.
Results emerge when thinking is clear, feeling is aligned, decisions are coherent, and behaviour is disciplined. When any part of the chain is weak, execution begins to leak.
CHAIN_QUOTE: “Strategy does not jump from intention to outcome. It moves through people. It is interpreted through thinking, experienced through feeling, converted through deciding, and delivered through behaving.”
